# How many acoustic panels do I need?

> Estimate acoustic panel count using either wall-coverage percentage (when room reverberation time is unmeasured) or the Sabine RT60 room-absorption model.

## Calculator
- [Open the calculator](https://howmanyacousticpanelsdoineed.com/): US room coverage: a 16 × 12 × 8 ft room (448 sq ft walls) at 20% coverage needs 89.6 sq ft, or 12 standard 4 × 2 ft panels. Metric coverage: a 5 × 4 × 2.5 m room (45 m² wall area) at 20% moderate coverage needs 9.0 m² of treatment, or 13 panels of 1.2 × 0.6 m.

## Guide
- [How to work out how many acoustic panels you need](https://howmanyacousticpanelsdoineed.com/guide/): step-by-step measuring, common mistakes, and ordering checklist.

## Formula and method
Coverage mode: Panels = ceiling((2 × (L + W) × H × coverage% / 100) / (panel W × panel H)). Sabine mode: ΔA = 0.161 × V × (1 / T_target − 1 / T_current); Panels = ceiling(ΔA / (panel area × (α_panel − α_surface))).

In Coverage % mode, calculate total wall surface area, apply your target coverage percentage (10%–15% light, 15%–25% moderate, 25%–40% heavy), and divide by single-panel area. In Sabine RT60 mode, infer current and target absorption from room volume and measured reverberation time using T = 0.161 × V / A, then divide required added absorption by net absorption per panel.

## Limits
Acoustic panels reduce echo and reverberation inside the room—they do not soundproof walls between rooms. A single NRC number hides weak low-frequency absorption on thin panels. Sabine assumes a diffuse sound field; room modes, bass traps, furniture, and first-reflection placement require separate attention.

## Room treatment coverage targets and panel material NRC ratings

Thicker fibrous panels absorb lower voice and music frequencies far better than thin decorative foam.

| Treatment level or panel type | Target wall coverage / NRC | Typical RT60 goal | Acoustic performance note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Light (living room / home office) | 10% – 15% of wall area | 0.6 – 0.8 s | Tames slap echo on voice calls |
| Moderate (conference / podcast room) | 15% – 25% of wall area | 0.4 – 0.6 s | Clear speech intelligibility |
| Heavy (recording studio / home theater) | 25% – 40% of wall area | 0.25 – 0.4 s | Pair wall panels with corner bass traps |
| 1 in (25 mm) acoustic foam | NRC ~0.40 – 0.60 | — | High frequencies only; minimal bass control |
| 2 in (50 mm) mineral wool / fiberglass | NRC ~0.80 – 0.95 | — | Strong voice & mid-high broadband absorption |
| 4 in (100 mm) broadband / bass trap | NRC ~0.95 – 1.00+ | — | Extends effective control into low-mids |
| Wood slat + felt backing (on wall) | NRC ~0.45 – 0.75 | — | Higher NRC (~0.80+) when mounted over battens + wool |

## Step by step
1. Measure room length, width, and ceiling height in feet or meters.
2. If you have not measured your room reverberation time, use Coverage % mode: 10% to 15% of wall area for light echo control in offices, 15% to 25% for meeting or podcast rooms, and 25% to 40% for critical studios.
3. If you have measured your current RT60 reverberation time (for example with a measurement microphone or clap-decay app), switch to Sabine RT60 mode and enter current RT60, target RT60, and panel NRC/absorption values.
4. Enter the dimensions of the panels you plan to hang (common broadband panels are 4 × 2 ft or 120 × 60 cm).

## Common mistakes
- Buying absorption panels expecting to block traffic noise or noisy neighbors. Sound isolation requires mass, sealed air gaps, and decoupled walls—not surface panels.
- Buying thin 1-inch foam expecting bass control. Thin foam mainly absorbs high frequencies and can leave a room sounding dull yet boomy.
- Clustering every panel on one wall. Spreading panels across opposite walls and first-reflection points prevents flutter echo far more effectively.
- Treating a single NRC rating as equal across all frequencies—always check octave-band absorption data down to 125 Hz and 250 Hz.

## Worked examples
### Example 1
Metric coverage: a 5 × 4 × 2.5 m room (45 m² wall area) at 20% moderate coverage needs 9.0 m² of treatment, or 13 panels of 1.2 × 0.6 m.

### Example 2
US room coverage: a 16 × 12 × 8 ft room (448 sq ft walls) at 20% coverage needs 89.6 sq ft, or 12 standard 4 × 2 ft panels.

### Example 3
Sabine RT60 model: reducing a 50 m³ room from 1.2 s to 0.6 s with 0.80-absorption panels over 0.05 walls needs 6.71 m² added absorption (13 panels).
